catalog_quote: [p.69] 3.3.3 Accent/Stress in Tangwang. Having lost tone in monosyllabic words, Hui people use the accent opposition of high (H) and low (L) in dissyllabic words. ... If H and L are used to describe dissyllables in Tangwang, we can say that generally the H accent is on the syllable [sic: word missing in the Google Books the text]. In Chinese morphology, the suffix tsy is added to a word to form a noun. In Standard Mandarin, this suffix is atonal; in other words, the accent is on the first tonal syllable. However in Tangwang, the situation is reversed, and the suffix must be phonetically put in focus. Among Han people however, the pronunciation is more similar to Standard Mandarin: the suffix ts is not necessarily stressed. [p.70] ... dissyllabic words, the general tendency is LH and not the reverse. [p.75] ... Tangwang shows the same tendency. The L/H model can be described as 242, 442. ... Mongolic languages, Dongxiang does not possess a tone system. Liu Zhaoxiong (1981: 17) indicates that the Dongxiang language is a stress-final language: the stress is put on the last syllable. [p.76] ... It is clear that their stress pattern in Dongxiang is the same as in Tangwang (see Table 3.13). new_statements.rule_in_words: Among Hui (Muslim) speakers, lexical tone is lost on monosyllables and disyllabic words carry a Low-High accent pattern, i.e. prominence (H accent/stress) on the final syllable, even on the nominal suffix -tsɿ that is toneless/unstressed in Standard Mandarin; the pattern matches stress-final Dongxiang. Han speakers in Tangwang keep a reduced (2-3) tone system and do not necessarily stress the suffix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing seen in the accessible snippets.
new_statements.exceptions: 'general tendency is LH and not the reverse' (so not exceptionless); Han speakers pattern more like Standard Mandarin (suffix -tsɿ not necessarily stressed); speakers told the author context, not stress, disambiguates disyllabic homophones (p.74); one Han informant uses three tones (fn.31).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern disyllabic words in citation/reading forms and a perception test of disyllabic homophones (Tables 3.11-3.13); described as an H/L 'accent' opposition replacing tone rather than classic dynamic stress. Access was via page-numbered Google Books snippets; one snippet sentence reads 'generally the H accent is on the syllable' with a word apparently missing in the printed text, so the LH/final reading rests on pp. 70 and 76.
new_statements.identity_note: Xu 2017 describes the speech of Tangwang town (唐汪川), Dongxiang Autonomous County, Linxia Hui Prefecture, Gansu = Glottolog tang1373. The stress-final/LH statement applies specifically to Hui (Muslim, incl. converted Tang/Wang clans) speakers; Han speakers in the same villages are described as retaining a reduced 2-3-tone system closer to Hezhou/Linxia Mandarin. Djamouri (2022, 2025) treats the same variety as having three low-amplitude contrastive tones and regards the tone-vs-accent question as unresolved.

tone_statements.citation: Xu Dan 徐丹. 2017. 关于汉语声调的一些思考 [Some considerations on the tone in Chinese]. 南开语言学刊 (Nankai Linguistics) 2017(2) [总第30期]: 11-23. Author version on HAL, hal-01890765.
tone_statements.quote: [table, p.16] ７０）唐汪① ２ 徐丹，２０１４ [...] [p.16] 从图１不难看出，２声调出现的地方都和无声调的非汉语言毗邻。汉语受到非汉语的影响是毋庸置疑的。徐丹（２０１４）在唐汪曾做过几次试验唐汪回民由于单字调已经失去，，“单字听写完全是任意选字如他们听到碗”词时可以理解为碗玩万 [...] 但是他们在交流时却没有任何问题因为语境上下文提供了最，、好的信息。 [...] ①唐汪话里回民和汉民声调系统有差异请见徐丹，（２０１４）。
tone_statements.translation: [table] 70) Tangwang(1) - 2 [tones] - Xu Dan 2014. [...] From Map 1 it is easy to see that every place where a 2-tone system occurs borders on toneless non-Chinese languages; that Chinese has been influenced by non-Chinese languages is beyond doubt. Xu Dan (2014) ran several tests in Tangwang: because the Tangwang Hui have already lost monosyllabic (citation) tone, character choice in single-character dictation is entirely arbitrary - hearing 'wan' they may take it as 碗 'bowl', 玩 'play' or 万 'ten thousand' [...] yet in communication they have no problem at all, because context supplies the best information. [...] fn.1: In Tangwang the tone systems of the Hui and of the Han differ; see Xu Dan (2014).

sources.note: States 'there are to date no decisive studies on the number or even the existence of contrastive tones in Tangwang', criticising analyses that disregard 'the accentuation phenomena' words exhibit; cites Ran, Yu & Shi 2022 and Li Lan 2022 for competing tone analyses. No stress-position rule.
